en: One day Sophie and her cousin Paul were playing in their room;
they were having fun catching the flies that were walking about on the windowpanes;
as they caught them, they put them in a little paper box that their papa had made for them.
When they had caught lots of them, Paul wanted to see what they were doing in the box.
"Give me the box," he said to Sophie, who was holding it; "let's look at what the flies are doing."
Sophie gave it to him; very carefully they half opened the little door of the box.
Paul put his eye to the opening and cried:
"Oh, how funny! How they're moving about! They're fighting; there's one pulling a leg off its friend… the others are angry…
Oh, how they're fighting! There are some falling down! Now they're getting up again…"
"Let me have a look now, Paul," said Sophie.
Paul didn't answer and went on looking and describing what he saw.
Sophie was getting impatient; she took hold of a corner of the box and pulled very gently;
Paul pulled on his side; Sophie got cross and pulled a little harder;
Paul pulled harder still; Sophie gave the box such a jerk that she tore it.
All the flies rushed out and landed on the eyes, cheeks and noses of Paul and Sophie, who chased them away by slapping themselves hard.
"It's your fault," Sophie said to Paul; "if you had been nicer, you would have given me the box and we wouldn't have torn it."
"No, it's your fault," answered Paul; "if you had been less impatient, you would have waited for the box and we would still have it."
You're selfish; you only think of yourself.
And you lose your temper like the turkeys on the farm.
I don't lose my temper at all, sir; I just think you're nasty.
I'm not nasty, miss; I'm just telling you the truth, and that's why you're red with rage like the turkeys with their red wattles.
I don't want to play any more with a nasty boy like you, sir.
I don't want to play with a nasty girl like you either, miss."
And they both went off to sulk, each in a corner.
Sophie soon got bored, but she wanted to make Paul believe she was having a wonderful time;
so she began to sing and to catch more flies;
but there weren't many left, and the ones that remained wouldn't let themselves be caught.
Suddenly she spots with delight a big bee sitting very still in a little corner of the window.
Sophie knew that bees sting, so she didn't try to catch it with her fingers;
she took her handkerchief out of her pocket, put it over the bee and grabbed it before the poor creature had time to escape.
Paul, who was bored too, was watching Sophie and saw her catch the bee.
"What are you going to do with that creature?" he asked her.
Leave me alone, you nasty boy; it's none of your business.
I beg your pardon, Miss Furious; I do beg your pardon for speaking to you and for forgetting that you were badly brought up and rude.
I'll tell Mama, sir, that you think I'm badly brought up; since she's the one bringing me up, she'll be very pleased to hear it.
No, Sophie, don't tell her: I'd get told off.
Yes, I will tell her; if you get told off, so much the better; I'll be very glad.
You're horrid! I won't say another word to you."
And Paul turned his chair round so as not to see Sophie, who was delighted to have frightened Paul and went back to her bee.
Very gently she lifted a little corner of the handkerchief, squeezed the bee a little between her fingers through the handkerchief to stop it flying away, and took her little knife out of her pocket.
"I'm going to cut its head off," she said to herself, "to punish it for all the stings it has given."
And so Sophie put the bee on the floor, still holding it through the handkerchief, and with one stroke of the knife she cut off its head;
then, since she found it great fun, she went on cutting it into pieces.

She was so busy with the bee that she didn't hear her mother come in; seeing her on her knees and almost motionless, her mother crept up to see what she was doing, and saw her cutting off the poor bee's last leg.
Outraged at Sophie's cruelty, Madame de Réan pulled her ear hard.
Sophie gave a cry, jumped to her feet and stood trembling in front of her mother.
"You are a wicked girl, miss; you're making this creature suffer in spite of what I told you when you salted and cut up my poor little fish…
I forgot, Mama, honestly.

I'll make you remember, miss: first by taking away your knife, which I won't give back for a year, and then by making you wear these pieces of the bee round your neck, threaded on a ribbon, until they fall to dust."

However much Sophie prayed and begged her mother not to make her wear the bee as a necklace, her mother called the nanny, had a black ribbon brought, threaded the pieces of the bee on it and tied them round Sophie's neck.
Paul didn't dare say anything; he was dismayed; when Sophie was left alone, sobbing and ashamed of her necklace, Paul tried to comfort her in every way he could;

he kissed her, asked her to forgive him for saying silly things, and tried to make her believe that the bee's yellow, orange, blue and black colours looked very pretty, like a necklace of jet and jewels.
Sophie thanked him for his kindness; she was a little comforted by her cousin's friendship, but she was still very upset about her necklace.
For a week the pieces of the bee stayed whole; but at last, one fine day, Paul, playing with her, crushed them so thoroughly that there was nothing left but the ribbon.
He ran to tell his aunt, who allowed him to take off the black cord.
That is how Sophie got rid of it, and after that she never made any animal suffer again.
pt: Um dia, a Sophie e o primo Paul brincavam no quarto;
divertiam-se a apanhar as moscas que passeavam pelos vidros da janela;
à medida que as apanhavam, metiam-nas numa caixinha de papel que o pai lhes tinha feito.
Quando já tinham apanhado muitas, o Paul quis ver o que elas faziam dentro da caixa.
— Dá-me a caixa — disse ele à Sophie, que a segurava —; vamos ver o que fazem as moscas.
A Sophie deu-lha; entreabriram com muito cuidado a portinha da caixa.
O Paul encostou o olho à abertura e exclamou:
— Ah, que engraçado! Como elas se mexem! Estão a lutar; ali está uma a arrancar uma pata à amiga… as outras estão zangadas…
Oh, como lutam! Ali estão algumas a cair! E agora levantam-se…
— Deixa-me olhar agora a mim, Paul — disse a Sophie.
O Paul não respondeu e continuou a olhar e a contar o que via.
A Sophie impacientava-se; pegou numa ponta da caixa e puxou devagarinho;
o Paul puxou do lado dele; a Sophie zangou-se e puxou um pouco mais;
o Paul puxou ainda com mais força; a Sophie deu um tal esticão à caixa que a rasgou.
As moscas todas saíram disparadas e pousaram nos olhos, nas faces e no nariz do Paul e da Sophie, que as enxotavam dando grandes palmadas a si próprios.
— A culpa é tua — dizia a Sophie ao Paul —; se tivesses sido mais simpático, tinhas-me dado a caixa e não a tínhamos rasgado.
— Não, a culpa é tua — respondia o Paul —; se tivesses sido menos impaciente, tinhas esperado pela caixa e ainda a tínhamos.
És egoísta, só pensas em ti.
E tu ficas furiosa como os perus da quinta.
Eu não fico nada furiosa, senhor; só acho que é mau.
Não sou mau, menina; só lhe digo a verdade, e é por isso que está vermelha de raiva como os perus com as suas cristas vermelhas.
Não quero brincar mais com um rapaz mau como o senhor.
Nem eu quero brincar com uma menina má como a menina.
E os dois foram amuar, cada um para o seu canto.
A Sophie depressa se aborreceu, mas quis fazer crer ao Paul que se estava a divertir muito;
pôs-se então a cantar e a apanhar mais moscas;
mas já não havia muitas, e as que restavam não se deixavam apanhar.
De repente, vê com alegria uma abelha grande que estava muito quieta num cantinho da janela.
A Sophie sabia que as abelhas picam; por isso não tentou apanhá-la com os dedos;
tirou o lenço do bolso, pô-lo em cima da abelha e agarrou-a antes de o pobre bicho ter tempo de fugir.
O Paul, que também se aborrecia, olhava para a Sophie e viu-a apanhar a abelha.
— Que vais fazer a esse bicho? — perguntou-lhe ele.
Deixa-me em paz, mau, não tens nada com isso.
Desculpe, menina furiosa, peço-lhe muita desculpa por lhe ter falado e por me ter esquecido de que era mal-educada e impertinente.
Vou dizer à mamã, senhor, que me acha mal-educada; como é ela que me educa, vai ficar muito contente por saber.
Não, Sophie, não lhe digas: ralhavam comigo.
Digo, sim; se ralharem contigo, tanto melhor; fico muito contente.
Má, é o que tu és! Não te digo nem mais uma palavra.
E o Paul virou a cadeira para não ver a Sophie, que estava encantada por ter assustado o Paul e voltou a ocupar-se da abelha.
Levantou devagarinho uma pontinha do lenço, apertou um pouco a abelha entre os dedos através do lenço, para a impedir de voar, e tirou do bolso o seu canivete.
— Vou cortar-lhe a cabeça — disse para si —, para a castigar por todas as picadas que deu.
E assim a Sophie pousou a abelha no chão, sempre a segurá-la através do lenço, e com um golpe de canivete cortou-lhe a cabeça;
depois, como achou aquilo muito divertido, continuou a cortá-la aos bocadinhos.

Estava tão ocupada com a abelha que não ouviu a mãe entrar; esta, ao vê-la de joelhos e quase imóvel, aproximou-se devagarinho para ver o que ela fazia, e viu-a a cortar a última pata da pobre abelha.
Indignada com a crueldade da Sophie, a senhora de Réan puxou-lhe a orelha com força.
A Sophie soltou um grito, levantou-se de um salto e ficou a tremer diante da mãe.
— É uma menina má, menina; faz sofrer este bicho apesar de tudo o que lhe disse quando salgou e cortou os meus pobres peixinhos…
Esqueci-me, mamã, garanto-lhe.

Pois eu faço-a lembrar-se, menina: primeiro, tirando-lhe o canivete, que só lhe devolvo daqui a um ano, e depois obrigando-a a usar ao pescoço estes bocados da abelha enfiados numa fita, até se desfazerem em pó.

Por mais que a Sophie pedisse e suplicasse à mãe que não a obrigasse a usar a abelha como colar, a mãe chamou a ama, mandou vir uma fita preta, enfiou os bocados da abelha e atou-os ao pescoço da Sophie.
O Paul não se atrevia a dizer nada; estava consternado; quando a Sophie ficou sozinha, a soluçar e envergonhada do colar, o Paul tentou consolá-la de todas as maneiras possíveis;

beijava-a, pedia-lhe desculpa por lhe ter dito parvoíces e queria fazê-la acreditar que as cores amarela, laranja, azul e preta da abelha faziam um efeito muito bonito e pareciam um colar de azeviche e pedras preciosas.
A Sophie agradeceu-lhe a bondade; ficou um pouco consolada com a amizade do primo, mas continuou muito desgostosa com o colar.
Durante uma semana, os bocados da abelha ficaram inteiros; mas por fim, num belo dia, o Paul, ao brincar com ela, esmagou-os tão bem que só ficou a fita.
Correu a avisar a tia, que lhe deu licença para tirar o cordão preto.
Foi assim que a Sophie se livrou dele, e desde então nunca mais fez sofrer nenhum animal.
